# Notes on Hosea 7 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**How far I got.** I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Precept Austin (only part of the page loaded), the Pulpit Commentary in full for vv. 1–8, Calvin on CCEL, and the Bible Hub and StudyLight pages that collect older commentators (Gill, Clarke, Barnes, Henry, Keil & Delitzsch, and others). I found nothing from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org's notes, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out. The notes for vv. 9–16 are thinner than for vv. 1–8.

**On section 2 (Protestant traditions).** The disagreements I found are about what the text means. They don't split along church lines: commentators from the same tradition disagree with each other, and ones from different traditions agree. Where I give a commentator's tradition, it's to help you place them, not to suggest a denominational position.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading (Guzik):** God was willing to heal Israel from their sin and its effects, but not as long as they acted as if God did not see their sin. They had to treat God as He really is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Precept Austin:** God's attempts to heal only brought more sin into the open. The light of God's Word did not create their sin but revealed it, exposing what had long been concealed and leaving them without excuse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary
- **Pulpit Commentary, three views of the "healing":** (1) the prophets' warnings and rebukes; (2) more likely, the partial return of national prosperity under Jeroboam II; (3) Jerome's view, which Pulpit finds less natural. Jerome took the old sin to be the golden calf in the wilderness and the new idols to be Jeroboam's calf-worship. Pulpit also compares the verse to a wound whose danger is only revealed when the surgeon probes it to heal it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
- **Matthew Henry:** "falsehood" could mean idol-worship, cheating one another, or, as he prefers, faking repentance before God. They say that they are desirous to be healed by him... but they lie unto him with their mouth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_007.cfm
- **Trent Butler (quoted by Precept Austin):** the verb is the "false witness" verb of Exodus 20:16, here used of political promises and alliances made with no intention of keeping them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary

**v. 2**
- **Guzik:** The problem among the people and leaders of Israel was they forgot – willfully – that the LORD saw and remembered their sin. He sets this against the new-covenant promise that God will remember sins no more (Jeremiah 31:34). Time doesn't make God forget sin; only the atoning substitute of Jesus does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Matthew Henry:** till God by pardoning our sins has cast them behind his back, they are still before his face. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_007.cfm
- **Pulpit:** when God "remembers" wickedness, that means he will punish it. "Their deeds surround them" could mean the sins are plainly visible, like a robe the person wears. Or it could mean the consequences close in like an army besieging a city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
- **Bible Hub study page:** the Hebrew word for "remember" (*zakar*) implies an active, mindful awareness. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/hosea/7.htm

**v. 3**
- **Guzik:** this verse, together with vv. 5 and 7, probably all refer to one of the successful assassination plots against the throne of Israel. Four kings were overthrown during Hosea's ministry, so it's hard to say which. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Pulpit, two readings:** (1) the king and princes enjoyed the crimes of low men, or enjoyed hearing them told (Abarbanel's view); (2) the plotters made the king merry with wine so they could murder him while pretending friendship. Pulpit says the second fits the context well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:** Israel was inflamed with desire and passion after idols like the coals of a freshly stoked fire. He links this to Paul's "burn with passion" in 1 Corinthians 7:9. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Literal or spiritual adultery? The commentators differ:**
  - **Gill (Baptist):** both. "All" means king, princes, priests and people, who were idolaters and also given to physical adultery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm
  - **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran scholars):** "all" means the whole nation. The word means spiritual adultery, apostasy from the Lord; and literal adultery is only so far to be thought of, that the worship of Baal promoted licentiousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm
  - **Matthew Poole:** puts the stress on physical adultery among the courtiers and people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** the image shows the people weren't corrupted by pressure from outside but by their own inclination and propensity of mind. The fire had been building for a long time, not suddenly lit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-4.html
- **Who is the baker?**
  - **Pulpit:** either a spirit of treason (compare the "spirit of whoredoms" in Hosea 5:4) or the ringleaders who used others as tools. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
  - **Barnes and Gill:** bring in Satan or the devil as the one who stirs the fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm
  - **Utley (bible.org):** the image is either of plotters rising early to plan treason, or of bakers who neglect their work and ruin the bread. https://bible.org/seriespage/hosea-7

**v. 5**
- **Meaning of "the day of our king":**
  - **Pulpit:** the king's birthday, his accession anniversary, or ironically the day he is destroyed. "Our" may be the fake loyalty of the traitors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
  - **Utley:** possibly an annual coronation celebration, a birthday celebration, or a special day honoring a military victory. https://bible.org/seriespage/hosea-7
- **Pulpit:** the princes got the king drunk for two reasons: to fire themselves up for murder and to leave him helpless. "Stretched out his hand with scorners" means he joined their drunken party as an equal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The scoffers are drunkards, just as in Proverbs 20:1 wine is directly called a scoffer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/hosea-7.html
- **Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary:** Those who tempt others to drunkenness never can be their real friends, and often design their ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm

**v. 6**
- **Precept Austin:** the plotters hid their murderous plans like embers hidden beneath ashes, and by morning the plot broke out into violence. The lesson drawn: unchecked anger and cherished sin never remain dormant. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary
- **Pulpit:** the heart is the oven, sinful passion is the fire, and the murder plot is the fuel. The baker "sleeps" only while the dough rises. Pulpit also notes this is a hard verse: one scholar (Wünsche) calls it perhaps the hardest in the book. Some read "their anger" in place of "their baker," but Pulpit keeps the usual reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Lust in the heart is like fire in an oven. Those who make themselves fiery ovens by their own passions will, unless grace puts the fire out, be made a fiery oven by God's wrath (Psalm 21:9; Malachi 4:1). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-4.html

**v. 7**
- **Clarke (Wesleyan/Methodist):** Zechariah was slain by Shallum; Shallum, by Menahem; Pekahiah, by Pekah; and Pekah, by Hoshea, 2 Kings 15:8-30. All were idolaters, and all came to an untimely death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-7.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch take a different line:** "all their kings have fallen" takes in every earlier revolution as well. They see no foundation whatever for the widespread historical interpretation of these verses, as relating to a conspiracy against the then reigning king. They take the "baker" to be the passion for idolatry, not a particular plotter. This differs from Guzik, Pulpit and Precept Austin, who read vv. 3–7 as a palace plot. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/hosea-7.html
- **Guzik on "none calls upon Me":** Israel still offered sacrifices to God (Hosea 5:6), but it was empty ceremony, not a true calling upon their covenant God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Precept Austin (quoting *Today in the Word*):** God wasn't ignoring their cries—there were none to be heard. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary
- **Pulpit:** "calling unto" God means crying to him for rescue, which is different from "calling on the name" of the LORD in worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** In thinking they can serve both the Lord and idols, Israel is like an unturned pancake – burned on one side, uncooked on the other. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Pulpit:** the best commentary on "mixed himself" is Psalm 106:35–39, where Israel mingled with the nations and served their idols. https://biblehub.com/hosea/7-8.htm
- **Ellicott:** the cake is burnt on one side to a cinder, and on the other left in a condition utterly unfit for food. https://biblehub.com/hosea/7-8.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** his emphasis is a little different. The point is that Ephraim was inconstant and unreliable, like the French saying "neither flesh nor fish." https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom26.xiv.xi.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** uses the same proverb, saying Ephraim had brought pagan superstition into worship and so was "nothing in religion." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/hosea/7-8.html
- **Barnes:** God would amend them, and they, withholding themselves from His discipline, and not yielding themselves wholly to it, were but spoiled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-8.html
- **Clarke:** describes the Eastern way of baking cakes on a heated hearth under embers, turning them several times. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-8.html
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** stresses that God had forbidden mixing with the pagan nations, so this is covenant-breaking. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-8.html
- **Precept Austin:** links "mixed up" to Hoshea's confused alliances. In 732 BC he switched from Egypt and its allies to Assyria, then later went back to Egypt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** Israel is as foolish as an old man who thinks and acts like he is still young. He compares Samson, who didn't know the LORD had left him (Judges 16:20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **G. Campbell Morgan (via Precept Austin):** asks Can any condition be conceived of more tragic than that of this disease and decay of which the sufferer is all unconscious? https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-7-commentary
- **Gaebelein:** the foreigners Israel mingled with drained its strength, and the gray hairs are signs of fast national decline that Israel failed to notice. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/gab/hosea-7.html?print=yes#1

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** they should have known, since even the pride of Israel testifies to his face – yet in their blind ignorance they do not return to the LORD their God. He cites Jeremiah 17:9 on how the heart deceives itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/

**v. 11**
- **Guzik:** Israel is like a confused, fluttering bird. They think they can escape God by running to other nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/
- **Pulpit:** groups vv. 8–11 as an attack on Israel's harmful foreign policy, as opposed to the internal corruption of vv. 1–7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html

**v. 12**
- **Clarke:** God will let them be caught by the very nations they trusted. The image of catching birds continues from the dove of v. 11. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-7.html
- **Translation note:** Guzik works from the NKJV's "according to what their congregation has heard," not the BSB's "when I hear them flocking together." He takes it to mean Greater knowledge means great accountability (compare Luke 12:48). You may want to flag the different wording for readers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/

**v. 13**
- **Guzik (on vv. 13–16):** Israel saw their problem, but not their sin. When God's hand is against man, he easily sees he has a problem but often does not see it as sin against the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-7/

**v. 14**
- **"Wail upon their beds":**
  - **Ellicott:** God discriminates between a heart-cry to Him, and a howl of despair, resembling the yell of a wild beast. A howl upon their bed is not a sob of true repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-14.htm
  - **Preacher's Homiletical Commentary:** Their tears were wrung from them on account of distress and not sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/hosea-7.html
- **"Assemble" or "slash themselves"? This is the main disputed point in the chapter:**
  - **Matthew Henry:** they held a solemn assembly for the sake of appearances, praying only for grain and wine during a drought. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hsa/Hsa_007.cfm
  - **Clarke:** they gathered not to seek God but to invoke their false gods for corn and wine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-7.html
  - **Ellicott:** some read "they assemble" as praying to the LORD for harvests, while others read "they excite themselves." The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) has "they cut themselves." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-14.htm
  - **Coffman:** calls the Hebrew text difficult and pictures Baal worship at a place like Bethel. He says gashing oneself was a real pagan practice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hosea/7-14.html
  - **Calvin:** gives two explanations. He rejects the one where they grew careless once the markets were full again, calling it too frigid and strained. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom26.xiv.xviii.html
- **"Turn away from Me":** Barnes says the Hebrew literally means "turn aside against Me," as if flying, as it were, in the very face of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Only one comment found. Pulpit describes the verse as Israel's "God-defying attitude," which v. 16 then pictures as a faulty bow. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html

**v. 16**
- **What makes the bow faulty?**
  - **Pulpit:** it was badly made, or its string has lost its spring, so the arrow goes wide of the mark. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html
  - **Clarke:** an Eastern bow, curved like a C when unstrung, springs back if it isn't bent properly. He says he faced this danger himself and claims that not one commentator has hit the meaning of the passage. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-7.html
  - **Calvin:** Israel seemed to repent but was really withdrawing from God, for they were, he says, like a deceitful bow. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol26/htm/xiv.xv.htm
- **"Cursing (rage) of their tongue" and derision in Egypt:**
  - **Clarke:** they mocked God (v. 5), and now their fall will be mocked in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/hosea-7.html
  - **One commentator on the Bible Hub page:** takes the tongue's "rage" to be boasting about friendship with Egypt's king Shebaka. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-16.htm
  - **Another reading on the same page:** carries the verse forward to the cry "His blood be on us." This is a later Christian application you may want to handle with care. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-16.htm
  - **Pulpit's application:** asks whether the "deceitful bow" describes every Christian who trusts in their own strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html

---

**Catholic and Orthodox views.** I found nothing on newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only older Catholic voices I came across were quoted second-hand in Protestant works: Jerome on v. 1 (in Pulpit) and the Latin Vulgate's wording of v. 4 (in Benson, on Bible Hub). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hosea-7.html, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hosea/7-4.htm

**Modern scholarship.** I found no Bible Odyssey articles or NET Bible notes. The NET Bible's own wording appears only as translation quotes, for example "slash themselves" in v. 14. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/hosea/7-14.html
